San Diego
January 24, 1998

When he was Drug Enforcement Administration agent, Rene De La Cova he arrested Manuel Noriega.  Later,he became a criminal, serving prison time for stealing $760,000 in laundered drug money while a DEA agent in the Miami area. Now he is in San Diego County -- in the drug-testing business, with clients, that include the San Diego Transit and the cities of Carlsbad and Oceanside. De La Cova represents Drug Testing Network, which collects specimens for alcohol and drug tests.

The Vista-based company, is owned by De La Cova's wife, Theresa, also is a former DEA agent. DTN claims to be an inexpensive mobile service that sends samples to independent laboratories for testing. Theresa De la Cova was forced to resign in 1994 when her husband pleaded guilty to stealing the funds while working on an undercover drug sting, according to court records in Miami.

De La Cova was a supervisor of the DEA's Fort Lauderdale, Fla., office at the time of his arrest. He is on probation after being sentenced to a two-year federal prison term. (It isn't as though he were doing something dangerous -- like growing marijuana for sick people.) The 48-year-old former agent has reimbursed the government since the theft and served a partial term, records show. His wife was not accused of wrongdoing.

While there is nothing illegal about De La Cova working in the drug-testing field this raises questions about the credibility and thoroughness of the cities’ reference checks of drug-testing collection businesses. It also points to the lack of regulations in this part of a multibillion-dollar industry that generally is heavily scrutinized across the nation. A federal court order filed in Miami states: "As directed by his probation officer, De La Cova shall notify third parties of risks that may be occasioned by defendant's criminal record."

The federal Department of Transportation, which has initiated stringent drug-testing procedures for "safety sensitive" employees, has no licensing requirement for collection agencies.

Besides the drug-collection work, Drug Testing Network offers drug-education programs.

"Join the growing number of businesses that are saying NO to drugs in the workplace," says its brochure that helped win a contract with the city of Carlsbad.
